title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
description: The application owns the cache: it checks first, falls back to the database on a miss, and writes the result back itself. The most common caching pattern, and the one whose failure modes you should be able to name.

steps.text: The application asks the cache for the key and gets a value back. The database is never touched — this is the path most reads take, and why caching is the cheapest large win available.
The application asks the cache and gets nothing back.
It falls back to the database, which is authoritative but slower.
It writes the value into the cache with a TTL, so the next reader hits. Note the application does this — the cache is passive, which is what makes this 'cache-aside' rather than read-through.
A popular key expires. Not one request misses — every concurrent request for that key misses at the same moment.

All of them fall through to the database simultaneously. A key that was absorbing thousands of reads per second now sends thousands of queries at once, which is how a cache expiry becomes a database outage.
Fixes: let only one request rebuild the key while others serve stale, add jitter to TTLs so keys don't expire together, or refresh hot keys before they expire.
